title: Enforce a commit message format — and fill it in automatically
summary: Reject messages that do not follow Conventional Commits, then add a second hook that prepends the ticket id from your branch name so nobody has to type it.
mental_model: `prepare-commit-msg` runs before you edit and can write into the message file. `commit-msg` runs after and can accept or reject it. Both receive the path to the message file as their first argument.

steps.title: Write the validator
steps.why: `$1` is the path to a file containing the proposed message. Read it, test it, exit non-zero to reject. Note it skips merge and fixup messages — a validator that blocks `git merge` is a validator people disable.

write.content:
#!/bin/sh
# Enforce Conventional Commits: type(scope)?: subject

msg_file="$1"
subject=$(head -1 "$msg_file")

# Let git's own generated messages through.
case "$subject" in
  "Merge "*|"Revert "*|"fixup! "*|"squash! "*) exit 0 ;;
esac

if ! echo "$subject" | grep -qE '^(feat|fix|docs|refactor|test|chore|perf)(\([a-z0-9-]+\))?: .{6,}'; then
  echo "commit-msg: rejected: '$subject'" >&2
  echo "commit-msg: expected  <type>(<scope>): <subject of at least 6 chars>" >&2
  echo "commit-msg: types     feat fix docs refactor test chore perf" >&2
  exit 1
fi

if [ ${#subject} -gt 72 ]; then
  echo "commit-msg: subject is ${#subject} characters, keep it under 72" >&2
  exit 1
fi

exit 0

steps.title: Watch a sloppy message get rejected
steps.why: 'fixed stuff' tells a future reader nothing. The hook refuses it before the commit object is created, so there is nothing to amend afterwards.
steps.expect: The hook's explanation and exit code 1.

steps.title: And an over-long one
steps.why: A subject that runs past 72 characters is truncated in every tool that shows a log. The check is trivial and the benefit compounds across thousands of commits.
commands: git commit -m "feat(pump): raise the pump speed to sixteen hundred revolutions per minute for the new impeller assembly"

verify.label: the over-long subject was rejected too

steps.title: Write one that passes
steps.why: Type, scope, imperative subject. Machine-readable enough for a changelog generator, human-readable enough to scan.
commands: git commit -m "feat(pump): raise speed to 1600 RPM for the new impeller"

steps.title: Stop typing the ticket id
steps.why: `prepare-commit-msg` runs before the editor opens and can rewrite the message file. Here it extracts the ticket from the branch name and appends it as a trailer — the information was already there, so a human should not have to retype it.

write.content:
#!/bin/sh
# Append a Refs: trailer taken from the branch name, e.g. feature/ABH-204-thing

msg_file="$1"
source="$2"

# Do not touch merges, squashes, or an amend of an existing message.
case "$source" in
  merge|squash|commit) exit 0 ;;
esac

branch=$(git symbolic-ref --quiet --short HEAD 2>/dev/null) || exit 0
ticket=$(echo "$branch" | grep -oE '[A-Z]+-[0-9]+' | head -1)
[ -n "$ticket" ] || exit 0

if ! grep -q "Refs: $ticket" "$msg_file"; then
  printf '\nRefs: %s\n' "$ticket" >> "$msg_file"
fi

exit 0

commands: git commit -m "feat(dosing): add calibrated dose calculation"
steps.expect: The message you typed, plus a Refs: ABH-204 trailer you did not.

verify.label: the ticket was added automatically from the branch name

steps.title: Confirm it is machine-readable
steps.why: Because it is a proper trailer, `%(trailers)` extracts it. Your changelog generator, release notes and ticket-linking now work without anyone changing their habits.

verify.label: the trailer parses as structured data

steps.title: Share both hooks
steps.why: Same pattern as any hook: track them and point `core.hooksPath` at the directory. A format nobody can install is a format nobody follows.

actions.run: git commit -q -m "chore(hooks): track commit message hooks"

verify.label: both hooks are tracked in the repository
no sloppy message reached history
verify.hint: the commit-msg hook must exit non-zero to reject

verify.label: the ticket trailer is generated from the branch name
both hooks are tracked so the team gets them

pitfalls: Always let `Merge`, `Revert`, `fixup!` and `squash!` messages through. A validator that blocks them makes rebasing and merging impossible.
`commit-msg` receives a file path, not the message text. Read `$1`; do not expect it on stdin.
`prepare-commit-msg` also runs for merges and amends — check `$2` (the source) or you will corrupt generated messages.
Client-side message rules are advisory. If the format gates a release pipeline, validate it again in CI.
cheatsheet: the current branch, for ticket extraction
